specPoints.text: use the idea of momentum to explain safety features

primer.text: You already know that every moving object carries momentum, and that a force acting over a time changes it. This lesson puts that idea to work: seat belts, airbags, crumple zones and crash mats all manipulate one quantity — the time a collision lasts — to cut the forces a body feels.

lessons.title: Safety features in vehicles
lessons.opening: When a car stops abruptly, its passengers keep moving — and the faster that momentum is brought to zero, the harder the hit. Every safety device in a vehicle works the same trick: stretching out the stopping time so the force shrinks. This lesson follows that idea through seat belts, airbags and crumple zones.
keyPoints: Force equals the rate of change of momentum, so lengthening the collision time lowers the force the impact delivers.
Contact time is how long the person stays in touch with whatever they have hit.
Crumple zones, seat belts and airbags absorb impact energy by changing shape, stretching the duration of the force.
A stretched seat belt gives the passenger's momentum longer to fall to zero, cutting the force felt.
Airbags cushion passengers thrown forwards, and crumple zones crush deliberately at the front and rear to extend the stopping time.
A heavy, fast vehicle carries huge momentum, so only an extended contact time can keep its impact force down.

low.restatement: Longer collision time means smaller force: that one trade is what every vehicle safety feature makes.
low.analogy: Catching a ball by drawing your hands back as it arrives — the same catch spread over more time stings far less.
low.examPointer: Feature questions want the chain spelled out: contact time up, so force down, so injury risk down.

medium.restatement: Because force is the rate of change of momentum, the same momentum change spread over a longer interval arrives as a gentler force — the shared design goal of crumple zones, belts and airbags.
medium.analogy: Picture the momentum change as a fixed volume of water and the contact time as the pipe's width: a wider pipe delivers the same water with a gentler push.
medium.examPointer: Name the feature, state that it increases the contact time, then give the reduced force on the passenger — all three steps earn the marks.

check.stem: For a colliding passenger, the force felt is smaller when:

options.text: The collision is over in a shorter instant
options.explanation: A shorter contact time would raise the force, not lower it.

options.text: The passenger carries more momentum into the crash
options.explanation: More momentum means a bigger change to unload, which raises the force.

options.text: The collision time is stretched out
options.explanation: Force is the rate of momentum change, so spreading it over more time lowers the force.

options.text: The vehicle is made heavier
options.explanation: Extra mass enlarges the momentum; it does nothing to soften the impact.

check.stem: A seat belt protects its wearer mainly by:

options.text: Holding the passenger perfectly rigid so no stretch occurs
options.explanation: A rigid hold would remove the stretch that lengthens the stopping time.

options.text: Stretching a little, so the wearer's momentum takes longer to fall to zero
options.explanation: The slight stretch extends the contact time and cuts the peak force.

options.text: Increasing the wearer's forward momentum
options.explanation: The belt changes how quickly momentum is lost, not how much there is.

options.text: Keeping the passenger loose so the interior absorbs the hit
options.explanation: Loose passengers strike the interior; the belt's job is to hold them and stretch gently.

check.stem: Crumple zones protect the people inside a car by:

options.text: Making the car bounce back off the obstacle
options.explanation: The zones deform; they do not make the car rebound.

options.text: Keeping the bodywork undamaged in a crash
options.explanation: The zones are meant to deform — some damage is designed in.

options.text: Cutting the car's speed before contact happens
options.explanation: They act during the collision itself, not on the approach.

options.text: Crushing in a planned way, which extends how long the car takes to stop
options.explanation: The controlled crush lengthens the stop and lowers the force on the passengers.

check.stem: Vehicle safety features absorb impact energy chiefly by:

options.text: Changing shape
options.explanation: Deforming structures soak up the crash energy as they give way.

options.text: Adding mass to the vehicle
options.explanation: Extra mass would enlarge the momentum instead of absorbing energy.

options.text: Reducing the car's speed before the impact
options.explanation: These features work inside the collision, not before it.

options.text: Heating up the passenger compartment
options.explanation: Heat plays no designed role in the protection.

check.stem: A truck striking a wall at speed needs a very long contact time because:

options.text: Trucks are built with softer crumple zones than cars
options.explanation: Material softness is not the reason; the size of the momentum is.

options.text: Its large mass and high speed together give it enormous momentum
options.explanation: A huge momentum change must be spread over a long time to keep the force down.

options.text: Its momentum stays small even at high speed
options.explanation: A massive, fast truck carries an enormous momentum.

options.text: The wall decides how hard to push back
options.explanation: The impact force follows from the truck's momentum change and the contact time alone.

check.stem: State what is meant by contact time.
check.modelAnswer: It is the duration for which the person stays in touch with whatever they have struck — a soft, giving contact makes it longer.

check.stem: Name the three main safety features built into a vehicle.
check.modelAnswer: Seat belts, airbags and crumple zones — all absorb crash energy by deforming and all stretch the time over which the force acts.

check.stem: Explain why crumple zones leave a car looking more damaged than expected, even after a small collision.
check.modelAnswer: Crumple zones at the front and rear are built to deform on purpose; the deliberate crumpling extends the vehicle's stopping time, so the passengers feel a smaller force — the visible damage is the price of that gentler stop.

check.stem: A designer must choose between a rigid metal dashboard and a padded, deformable one. Use the idea of momentum to argue for the padded design.
check.modelAnswer: The padded surface lengthens the contact time when a passenger is thrown forward, so the same momentum change spreads over a longer interval; with force as the rate of change of momentum, the padded dash delivers a smaller force and a lower injury risk.

lessons.title: Crash mats
lessons.opening: Drop a ball on concrete and it stops in an instant; drop it on a cushion and the stop takes longer, so it feels gentler. Crash mats, playground floors and mats for light landings all apply that principle to falling bodies. This lesson shows how a soft surface buys a falling body extra contact time.
keyPoints: Gymnasium crash mats are thick and soft to soak up the shock a landing body delivers.
A soft landing keeps the body touching the mat for longer than a hard floor would.
The extended contact time lowers the rate of momentum change, so the landing force and the injury risk both shrink.
Playground cushioning works identically, lengthening the time a falling child spends in touch with the ground.
Lighter children can manage with thinner mats, and low falls need less cushioning than high ones.
Safety features lessen the chance of serious harm but cannot rule out injury altogether.

low.restatement: A soft mat stretches the landing out, and a longer landing means a smaller force.
low.analogy: Jumping into water instead of onto paving — the water gives way, so the same stop takes longer and hurts less.
low.examPointer: Match the mat to the fall: heavier bodies and bigger drops call for thicker cushioning.

medium.restatement: The mat cannot change how much momentum the falling body must lose — only how long losing it takes; force is that momentum change divided by the time, so more time means less force.
medium.analogy: Think of it as a payment plan: the same debt of momentum settled over more instalments takes smaller bites out of you.
medium.examPointer: Justify mat thickness with both factors — the faller's mass and the speed at touchdown — not with one alone.

check.stem: A crash mat protects a falling gymnast chiefly by:

options.text: Reducing the gymnast's momentum to nothing instantly
options.explanation: An instant stop would mean a huge force — the opposite of protection.

options.text: Making the gymnast lighter in mid-air
options.explanation: The mat acts on landing; it cannot change the gymnast's mass.

options.text: Lowering the gymnast's speed before touchdown
options.explanation: The mat waits below; it works during contact, not during the descent.

options.text: Extending the time the gymnast spends in contact with the mat
options.explanation: A longer contact time slows the rate of momentum change, so the force drops.

check.stem: Why can a child manage with a thinner mat than an adult?

options.text: A smaller mass brings less momentum, so less cushioning time is needed
options.explanation: With less momentum to unload, a thinner mat still keeps the force low.

options.text: Children's bones are more flexible than adults'
options.explanation: The reasoning is about momentum, not biology.

options.text: Thin mats work only for light users
options.explanation: Mats work for everyone; thickness must match the momentum involved.

options.text: Children always fall from lower heights
options.explanation: Height is a separate factor; the thinner mat here follows from mass.

check.stem: A playground's cushioned surface protects falling children by:

options.text: Stopping children from ever reaching the ground
options.explanation: Children still land; the surface changes how the landing unfolds.

options.text: Lengthening their contact time with the ground
options.explanation: More contact time spreads the momentum change and shrinks the force.

options.text: Reducing the children's weight
options.explanation: Weight is unchanged; the surface changes the timing of the stop.

options.text: Absorbing the children's momentum entirely
options.explanation: The momentum still falls to zero — just across a longer interval.

check.stem: Which landing calls for the thickest crash mat?

options.text: A small child hopping off the final step
options.explanation: Low mass and low speed make this a gentle landing.

options.text: A slow sideways slip from standing height
options.explanation: A low-velocity fall carries little momentum.

options.text: A heavy adult dropping from a great height
options.explanation: Large mass and high speed mean the biggest momentum change, needing the longest contact time.

options.text: A light gymnast landing from a low beam
options.explanation: A light body and a small drop add up to a low-impact landing.

check.stem: Thick mats are laid beneath bouldering walls because falls from the wall:

options.text: Carry enough momentum to need a long contact time on landing
options.explanation: A bouldering fall arrives with real speed, so a long, soft stop keeps the force safe.

options.text: Arrive more slowly than an ordinary stumble
options.explanation: Bouldering falls are quick — which is exactly why the mat is thick.

options.text: Gain no speed on the way down
options.explanation: Gravity accelerates the descent, which is part of why the stop is severe.

options.text: Need to be brought to rest as quickly as possible
options.explanation: Fast stops give big forces; the mat deliberately draws the stop out.

check.stem: Why are gymnasium crash mats thick and soft?
check.modelAnswer: So they can soak up the shock a landing body delivers and keep that body in touch with the mat for longer.

check.stem: Name one place besides a gymnasium that cushions falls, and state how its surface helps.
check.modelAnswer: Playgrounds use cushioned surfaces; the soft ground lengthens the child's contact time with the ground, so the impact force is smaller.

check.stem: Explain why a soft crash mat makes a landing safer than a hard floor.
check.modelAnswer: The mat stretches out the contact time, so the body's momentum changes over a longer interval; the rate of momentum change is smaller, so the peak landing force and the chance of injury both fall.

check.stem: A 50 kg climber topples from a bouldering wall and lands at 4 m/s. A thick mat brings them to rest in 0.2 s; a bare floor would stop them in 0.02 s. Calculate the climber's momentum at landing and the average stopping force for each surface, then compare the two.
check.modelAnswer: Momentum at landing is 50 × 4 = 200 kg·m/s. On the mat, F = 200 ÷ 0.2 = 1000 N; on the bare floor, F = 200 ÷ 0.02 = 10000 N. The mat's longer contact time makes its force ten times smaller.

glossary.definition: How long a person or body stays in touch with whatever it strikes; stretching it out softens the force.
A vehicle restraint that holds the passenger to the seat and stretches a little to draw out the stopping time.
A soft cushion deployed at the front of a car that catches a passenger flung forwards in a crash.
A region at the front or rear of a vehicle built to crumple on purpose, extending the time the car takes to stop.
The quantity mass × velocity carried by a moving object; force equals how quickly it changes.
A thick, soft mat that soaks up the shock of a landing and lengthens the contact time.
